paragraphs: A People to Complete Centralization of Government, or Which Divert Them from It

All democratic nations are led by instinct toward the centralization of government, but they do not move toward it to the same degree. That depends on particular circumstances, which can either help or hinder the natural results of this social condition. These circumstances are very numerous, and I shall mention only a few. Where men enjoyed liberty long before they became equal, the tendencies that free institutions gave them resist, up to a point, the inclinations that equality produces. The central power may add to its privileges among such a people, yet the private citizens of that community will never lose their independence entirely. But suppose equality of conditions arises among a people that has never known freedom, or that stopped knowing it long ago. This is the situation on the Continent of Europe. Then the nation’s old habits suddenly join, as if by a natural attraction, with the new habits and principles that its social condition has produced. All powers seem to rush of their own accord toward the center. They pile up there with astonishing speed, and the state at once reaches the outer limit of its strength, while private persons sink just as suddenly into the deepest weakness.

The English who emigrated three hundred years ago to found a democratic commonwealth on the shores of the New World had all learned, in their mother country, to take part in public affairs. They knew trial by jury. They were used to freedom of speech and of the press, to personal freedom, to the idea of rights and the practice of asserting them. They brought these free institutions and manly customs with them to America, and the institutions protected them from the encroachments of the state. So among the Americans it is freedom that is old, and equality that is comparatively recent. In Europe the reverse is happening. There equality was introduced by absolute power, under the rule of kings, and had already soaked into the habits of nations long before freedom had entered their thinking.

I have said that among democratic nations the idea of government comes naturally to the mind as a single, central power, and that the idea of intermediate powers is unfamiliar to them. This applies above all to democratic nations in which equality has triumphed through a violent revolution. The classes that managed local affairs have been swept away suddenly by the storm. The confused mass that remains has neither the organization nor the habits needed to take over that administration. So the state alone appears able to take on every detail of government, and centralization becomes, so to speak, the unavoidable condition of the country. Napoleon deserves neither praise nor blame for gathering almost all the administrative power of France into his own hands. After the nobility and the upper ranks of the middle classes vanished so abruptly, these powers passed to him as a matter of course, and it would have been nearly as hard for him to refuse them as to take them. The Americans have never felt any such necessity. They went through no revolution and have governed themselves from the beginning, so they never had to ask the state to act as their guardian for a time. Thus the progress of centralization among a democratic people depends not only on the progress of equality but also on the way equality was established.

At the start of a great democratic revolution, when hostilities have only just broken out between the different classes of society, the people try to centralize the public administration in the hands of the government, so as to tear the management of local affairs away from the aristocracy. Toward the end of such a revolution, by contrast, it is usually the defeated aristocracy that tries to hand the management of every affair over to the state. It dreads the tyranny of a people that has become its equal and, not infrequently, its master. So it is not always the same class that works to enlarge the prerogative of the government. But as long as the democratic revolution lasts, there is always some class in the nation, strong in numbers or in wealth, that its own particular passions or interests push toward centralizing the public administration. This comes in addition to the hatred of being governed by one’s neighbor, a feeling that is general and permanent among democratic nations. We may note that today the lower orders in England are straining with all their might to destroy local independence and to move the administration from every point on the circumference to the center, while the higher classes are working to keep it within its ancient bounds. I venture to predict that a time will come when exactly the opposite will happen.

These observations explain why the supreme power is always stronger, and private individuals weaker, among a democratic people that has gone through a long and difficult struggle to reach equality than in a democratic community whose citizens were equal from the start. The Americans prove the point conclusively. The inhabitants of the United States were never divided by privileges. They have never known the relation of master and inferior. Since they neither fear nor hate one another, they have never felt any need to call in the supreme power to manage their affairs. The Americans’ lot is unusual. From the aristocracy of England they took the idea of private rights and a taste for local freedom, and they have kept both, because they had no aristocracy to fight.

Education has always helped men defend their independence, and this is especially true in democratic ages. When all men are alike, it is easy to establish a single, all-powerful government, and instinct alone is enough to do it. But under the same conditions, men need a great deal of intelligence, knowledge, and skill to organize and sustain secondary powers. They need the same qualities to create, amid the citizens’ independence and individual weakness, free associations that are able to resist tyranny without destroying public order.

So among democratic nations the concentration of power and the subjection of individuals will grow in proportion to their ignorance as well as to their equality. It is true that in ages of imperfect civilization a government is often as short of the knowledge needed to impose despotism on a people as the people are short of the knowledge needed to throw it off. But the effect is not the same on both sides. However rude a democratic people may be, the central power that rules it is never entirely without cultivation. It readily draws to its own use whatever little cultivation the country has, and if necessary it can look for help elsewhere. So in a nation that is ignorant as well as democratic, a striking difference soon opens up between the intellectual capacity of the ruler and that of each of his subjects. That completes the easy concentration of all power in his hands. The administrative function of the state keeps expanding, because the state alone is competent to administer the country’s affairs. Aristocratic nations, however unenlightened, never present the same spectacle, because among them instruction is spread almost equally between the monarch and the leading members of the community.

The pasha who now rules Egypt found a population of exceedingly ignorant and equal men, and he has borrowed the science and skill of Europe to govern them. The sovereign’s personal accomplishments are thus joined to the ignorance and democratic weakness of his subjects. Complete centralization has been established without any obstacle, and the pasha has made the country his factory and its inhabitants his workmen.

I think extreme centralization of government eventually saps society, and so, after some time, weakens the government itself. But I do not deny that a centralized social power can carry out great undertakings with ease, within a given time and at a particular point. This is most true in war, where success depends far more on the ability to move all of a nation’s resources to one place than on how large those resources are. Hence it is chiefly in war that nations want, and often need, to increase the powers of the central government. All men of military genius like centralization, because it adds to their strength. All men with a genius for centralizing like war, because it forces nations to combine all their powers in the hands of the government. Thus the democratic tendency that leads men without pause to multiply the privileges of the state and to narrow the rights of private persons is much faster and steadier among those democratic nations whose position exposes them to great and frequent wars than among all the others.

I have shown how the fear of disorder and the love of well-being lead democratic nations, without their noticing it, to enlarge the functions of the central government. It seems to them the only power that is, in itself, strong, enlightened, and secure enough to protect them from anarchy. I would now add that every particular circumstance that makes the condition of a democratic community unsettled and precarious strengthens this general propensity and leads private persons more and more to sacrifice their rights to their tranquility. A people is therefore never so ready to enlarge the functions of central government as at the end of a long and bloody revolution. Such a revolution has torn property from its former owners, shaken every belief, and filled the nation with fierce hatreds, clashing interests, and warring factions. At such times the love of public tranquility becomes an indiscriminate passion, and the members of the community tend to form an immoderate devotion to order.

I have already examined several of the incidents that can help promote the centralization of power, but the chief cause remains to be noticed. The foremost of the accidental causes that can draw the management of all affairs into the ruler’s hands in democratic countries is the ruler’s own origin and his own inclinations. Men who live in ages of equality are naturally fond of central power and willing to extend its privileges. But suppose this same power faithfully represents their own interests and exactly mirrors their own inclinations. Then the confidence they place in it knows no bounds, and they think that whatever they give to it they are giving to themselves.

Administrative powers will always be drawn toward the center less easily and less quickly under kings who are still connected in some way with the old aristocratic order than under new princes. These are the children of their own achievements, and their birth, prejudices, inclinations, and habits seem to bind them inseparably to the cause of equality. I do not mean that princes of aristocratic origin who live in democratic ages make no attempt to centralize. I believe they pursue that goal as diligently as any others. For them the only advantages of equality lie in that direction. But their opportunities are fewer, because the community, instead of readily complying with their wishes, often obeys them reluctantly. In democratic communities the rule is that centralization must increase to the degree that the sovereign is less aristocratic. When an ancient line of kings stands at the head of an aristocracy, the sovereign’s natural prejudices agree perfectly with those of the nobility. The vices inherent in aristocratic communities then run freely and meet no corrective. The opposite is true when the offspring of a feudal stock is placed at the head of a democratic people. His education, habits, and associations constantly lead the sovereign to adopt the feelings that inequality of conditions suggests, while the people, by their social condition, tend just as constantly toward the customs that equality produces. At such times it often happens that the citizens seek to restrain the central power far less as a tyrannical power than as an aristocratic one. They stand firm in defending their independence, not only because they want to stay free, but above all because they are determined to stay equal. A revolution that overthrows an ancient royal family in order to put men of more recent growth at the head of a democratic people may weaken the central power for a time. But however anarchic such a revolution may look at first, we need not hesitate to predict that its final and certain consequence will be to extend and secure that power’s prerogatives. The first condition for success in centralizing the supreme power in a democratic community, indeed the only one, is to love equality, or to make men believe that you love it. Thus the science of despotism, once so complicated, is simplified and reduced, as it were, to a single principle.
